overview.headline: A three-amino-acid fragment of a natural hormone, tested against gut inflammation in mice.
overview.lede: KPV (lysine-proline-valine) is the tail end of alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone, a hormone your body makes. University labs have studied it in mouse colitis since the 2000s. No company has taken it into human trials, no regulator has approved it, and the vials sold online as KPV are unapproved products.

mechanism.intro: Thought to calm inflammation from inside immune and gut cells.

parts.name: Alpha-MSH tail
parts.text: Alpha-MSH switches off inflammatory signalling. KPV is its last three amino acids and, in mice, kept an anti-inflammatory effect even when the hormone's usual receptor (MC1R) did not work.

parts.name: PepT1 transport
parts.text: Gut cells pull small peptides inside through a transporter called PepT1. In cell and mouse work, KPV entered this way and damped the inflammatory switch NF-kB.

parts.name: What is unknown
parts.text: Whether any of this happens in people. Nobody has measured KPV in human blood or compared it with a placebo.

more.title: More: where KPV came from
paras: Alpha-MSH is a 13-amino-acid hormone best known for tanning. Researchers in Germany and the United States found that its last three amino acids carried much of its anti-inflammatory activity without the pigment effect, and tested the fragment in mouse colitis. Sources are listed under the Status tab.

results.headline: No human results exist. The evidence is mouse colitis.
results.lede: Two independent groups found that KPV reduced gut inflammation in mice. That is the whole evidence base.

stats.lbl: mouse colitis models in which KPV sped recovery (chemical DSS colitis and T-cell transfer colitis)
stats.src: Kannengiesser et al., Inflamm Bowel Dis 2008

items.t: In DSS colitis and a T-cell transfer model, KPV-treated mice regained weight sooner, had less inflammation on biopsy and lower colonic myeloperoxidase, an enzyme marker of inflammation. In mice lacking a working MC1 receptor, KPV rescued all treated animals from death during DSS colitis (Kannengiesser 2008).
Dalmasso and colleagues (2008) showed intestinal cells take KPV up through PepT1, that it lowered inflammatory cytokines, and that mice given it in drinking water had milder colitis.
Nothing. The FDA's compounding review found no human exposure data for KPV by any route, and no clinical trial has been published or registered.

more.title: More: why mouse colitis results rarely transfer
paras: Chemical colitis in mice is a short injury that heals within days; human inflammatory bowel disease is a lifelong immune condition. Many compounds that worked in DSS mice have failed in people, which is why animal data are a reason to run a trial, not a substitute for one.

effects.headline: Unknown in humans. No safety data exist.
effects.lede: No person has received KPV in a study, so there is no side-effect rate, no discontinuation rate and no list of common reactions.

disc.title: Stopping because of side effects
disc.text: Not applicable. No human study has given KPV.

unique.title: The specific risk: an unstudied peptide, usually injected
unique.text: KPV has not been linked to a particular toxicity, because nobody has looked. The FDA's stated concerns are immunogenicity (the immune system reacting to the peptide or to impurities) and the absence of any human exposure data. At the July 2026 advisory meeting its reviewers added that these peptides lack a settled chemical identity in commerce, so two products labelled KPV may not be the same substance.

more.title: More: what a trial would monitor for
paras: A Phase 1 study would track injection-site and allergic reactions, blood counts, liver and kidney tests, and blood levels of the peptide. None of that exists for KPV.

more.title: More: the good side effects
paras: None reported in humans. In mice the benefit was less gut inflammation.

urgent.title: Symptoms doctors treat as urgent after any injected product
items: Swelling of the face or throat, trouble breathing, hives
Fever, spreading redness or pus at an injection site
New or worsening abdominal pain, or bloody diarrhea
Dark urine, yellowing of the skin or eyes
urgent.note: Anyone with these symptoms should get medical care right away and bring the product with them.

levels.nopk: No one has measured KPV in human blood after a dose, so there is no half-life, no peak time and nothing to model. Peptides this small are usually broken down quickly by enzymes in blood and gut, but for KPV even that has not been documented in people.

stats.lbl: amino acids, one of the smallest peptides sold as a 'research chemical'
the only species in which KPV's effects have been measured

explain.t: The simulator on other pages uses a measured human half-life. None exists for KPV.

explain.b: Why vial labels tell you little.
explain.t: A milligram figure on a label is the seller's claim. Nobody independently tests these vials, and the FDA has said products sold as KPV may not even be the same substance.

more.title: More: what this page cannot tell you
paras: What a dose of KPV does in a human body, how long it lasts or what level is safe. Those questions are answered by Phase 1 trials, and none has been run.

trials.headline: No human trials have been run.
trials.lede: KPV has never been given to people in a registered study. The 2026 regulatory activity concerns whether pharmacies may compound it, and generated no clinical data.

more.title: More: what the FDA's advisory committee actually decided
paras: On July 23, 2026 the Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee voted 8 to 6, with one abstention, to recommend adding KPV to the list of substances pharmacies may compound under section 503A, against the advice of the FDA's own reviewers, who cited the lack of human data. The vote is advisory; the FDA must decide and, if it agrees, write a rule, which observers expect to take a year or more.

running.title: No human trials
items: None registered or published. The FDA found no human exposure data for KPV (list current April 22, 2026).
The July 2026 advisory vote concerns pharmacy compounding, not a trial.

find.text: If a trial is ever registered it will appear on the public registry. Searching today returns nothing for KPV as a treatment.

status.headline: Not approved anywhere. Off the FDA's 'do not compound' category since April 2026, but still unapproved and not yet compoundable.

items.label: Canada: not authorized
items.text: Health Canada has not authorized any KPV product. It treats injectable peptides as prescription drugs, said in April 2026 that unauthorized injectable peptide drugs are illegal in Canada, and in July 2026 obtained a permanent injunction against the Quebec seller Canlab Research.

items.label: US: not approved
items.text: The FDA has never approved KPV. In 2023 it placed KPV in 'Category 2' (significant safety concerns for compounding), citing no human exposure data. On April 15, 2026 the FDA announced its removal from that category; the list now shows the nomination as withdrawn.

items.label: US: compounding decision pending
items.text: On July 23, 2026 the FDA's advisory committee voted 8 to 6 to recommend KPV for the 503A bulks list. The FDA has not acted. Until it does, pharmacies have no clear legal basis to compound KPV, and no decision would make KPV an approved drug.

items.label: Sport: prohibited
items.text: Not named on the 2026 WADA Prohibited List, but its S0 clause bans at all times any substance with no approval anywhere for human use. KPV falls under it.

cards.title: What 'research use only' means
cards.text: Vials sold as KPV carry 'for research use only' labels. That describes a product meant for laboratory work, not people. It does not mean the contents were tested, and it does not make the sale legal once the seller markets the product for human use.
items: Health Canada: injectable peptides are prescription drugs; unauthorized ones are illegal to sell (2025 and 2026 notices).

FDA warning letters, August 24, 2026: the disclaimer does not control when a website shows the product is intended as a drug for people; selling bacteriostatic water and dose calculators alongside is evidence of intended human use.

cards.title: Symptoms to take to a doctor
cards.text: Anyone who has used a product sold as KPV should tell a doctor, especially with any of the following:
items: Fever, redness or pus at an injection site
Persistent abdominal pain or bloody stools
Dark urine, yellow skin or eyes
cards.note: Report a reaction to MedEffect Canada (canada.ca/medeffect) or, in the U.S., FDA MedWatch (fda.gov/medwatch).

more.title: More: Category 1, Category 2 and the 503A list
paras: The FDA sorts nominated bulk substances into Category 1 (may be compounded while review continues), Category 2 (may not) and a formal 503A list set by rule. KPV left Category 2 in April 2026 but was not placed in Category 1. Even a place on the 503A list would only let licensed pharmacies compound it on prescription; it would not be approval and would not establish a safe or effective dose.
